source_read: PDF, all 13 PDF pages (publisher's cover page, then online-first article pages 1–12): text read in full; Table 1 (rotated, pp. 5–6), Figure 1 (p. 3) and Figures 2–4 (pp. 7–9) checked on rendered pages; Figure 2–4 totals and every Table 1 fraction recomputed.

key_findings.note: p. 2: April 2017 search of PubMed, PsycINFO, CINAHL and Scopus, 1990–2017, one study added on updating to December 2017; selection criteria as stated (the exclusions also name 'reports').

Figure 1 (p. 3) and p. 2: 850, 144 duplicates, 706, 573 excluded, 133, 100 excluded, 1 added, 34, 11 excluded on appraisal, 23. Four excluded studies are named (Wood 2008, Leamon 2000, Lecomte 2013, Pollini and Strathdee 2007).
pp. 2–3: modified Hoy et al. (2012) tool, 10 items; all but Marshall et al. (2012) low risk; kappa 1.00; no per-study ratings anywhere in the paper.

p. 4: 17 USA (7 UC Davis Sacramento, 3 Hawaii), 1 Taiwan, 4 Australia, 1 Canada (sum 23, and Table 1 lists 17 US studies); linked sets and the 20-year repeat as stated. Which Oregon study Hendrickson et al. (2010) shares its data set with is ambiguous in the source; the card's wording is fair.
p. 4, Cardiac complications, 1st–2nd paragraphs: every number matches; the note (171 subjects in Table 1, p. 6) is right.

p. 7: police 57% (Pasic) and 12% (Richards 1999a); Szuster aggression 50%; Toles agitation and anxiety 48%; Pasic 48 (80%) of 60 psychotic and 12 depressed; Szuster 9 (64%), 12 (86%), 4 (29%), 1 (7%). The note's arithmetic is right: 12/60 = 20%; 9, 12, 4 and 1 of 14 give 64.3%, 85.7%, 28.6% and 7.1%.
Rotated Table 1 read on rendered pp. 5–6: every listed percentage matches its row.

Trauma presentations, 1st paragraph (p. 4) and 2nd paragraph (pp. 4 and 7): London 49%, 22%, 8.6%; Tominaga 36%, 17.9%, 3.6%. Minor and not on the card: Table 1 gives 'motor vehicle accidents 36%' to Schermer and Wisner and only 'intentional injury 37%' to Tominaga, so text and table do not line up on the trauma figures.

pp. 7–8 and Figure 2 (rendered p. 7): 17 studies; the Figure 2 totals sum to 120,111; 11.3% (6.3–19.7); 22.8% (15.4–32.5) against 5.7% (2.8–11.2), Q 12.42; settings 9.3%, 13.4%, 17.9%; the four denominators as stated; Hendrickson 2008 (353/15,308) and 2010 (714/37,625) both pooled. See missed: Richards et al. (1999a) enters with all 32,617 visits although Table 1 says 3,102 were urine-screened.

p. 8 and Figure 3: OR 1.422 (1.236–1.636); 23,434 men as printed (Figure 3 sums to 28,434) and 21,365 women; I² 50.16, Q 20.66, df 10, p = 0.029; toxicology interval 1.25–1.83 with no point estimate; settings 1.36, 2.22, 1.35.
pp. 8–9 and Figure 4: 1,597 and 40,545 (the plot's sample sizes sum to both); 28.4 against 38.4 years; OR 2.251 (1.421–3.567); 3.108, 2.228 and 1.286 (0.745–2.222; p = 0.367).

key_findings.correction: Two phrases are firmer than the source (p. 10). The authors say that a screen staying positive for 72 hours makes it difficult to link use accurately to the presentation (not that it cannot be tied to it), and that a lack of accurate assessment of time of last use prevents separating intoxication from withdrawal (not that time of last use was not recorded). Suggested end of the finding: '...that toxicology screens stay positive for 72 hours, which makes it difficult to link use to the acute presentation; and that time of last use was not accurately assessed, so intoxication cannot be separated from withdrawal in psychotic presentations.' The rest is confirmed. The same wording ('not assessed', 'cannot be tied') appears in the card's exposure fields.

Content confirmed: no study row and no part of the Results reports deaths or case fatality (the nearest item is Hawley's 'life-threatening complication 9%' in Table 1). Locator: mortality also appears on p. 1 (Introduction, 1st and 2nd paragraphs: mortality rate; premature death among long-term use), and the p. 2 paragraph on causes of death is the Introduction's 4th paragraph, the first that starts on p. 2 (METHODS §6.2). Suggested page and locator: 'pp. 1–10'; 'Introduction, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (p. 1) and 4th paragraph (p. 2); Results; Table 1 (pp. 5–6)'.

reporting_issues.note: Text p. 4: 36; Table 1 p. 6: all 171 subjects methamphetamine-positive.

p. 7 says nine studies used toxicology; p. 8 has 8 toxicology and 9 self-report. Besides Lee et al. (2009), Richards et al. (1999a) is also ambiguous: Table 1 gives 'urine screen and ED visits', and Figure 2 enters it with the all-visits denominator (461 of 32,617, 1.4%) rather than the 461 of 3,102 screened (14.9%).
30/133 = 22.6% and 557/6,193 = 9.0%; Figure 2 prints 0.226 and 0.090. Every other Table 1 fraction matches its printed percentage.
p. 4 (same data set; overlapping 2006–2007 periods) and Figure 2 (Cloutier 2013, Hendrickson 2008 and 2010 all pooled; their attendees are inside the 120,111).
p. 7 prints 12 (23%) of 60; p. 10 says nearly one-quarter depressed.
Table 1 (p. 6): 32 of 343; text p. 7: percentages consistent with 14 people.
The search section attributes the one added study to updating the search to December 2017 (p. 2), so the inconsistency may be one of labelling (update against hand search) rather than of numbers.

Facts confirmed: 18 distinct studies across Figures 2–4, Pasic et al. (2007), described in Table 1 as a case-control study using matched samples, only in Figures 3–4. The consequence is not right: an odds ratio comparing methamphetamine-positive with methamphetamine-negative people by sex or age is not distorted by sampling on methamphetamine status, and Pasic's sex OR 3.523 and age OR 2.445 show that its groups were not matched on sex or age (matching on them would force odds ratios near 1). Suggested consequence: 'Minor; the abstract's count of 17 understates the studies pooled, and the matching variables of the one case-control study are not stated.' The same correction applies to the card's comparison.matching field ('products of the design').
p. 4, Meta-analysis paragraph; no sensitivity result anywhere.

Reference list (p. 11): the title concerns ecstasy and related drug presentations at two Melbourne emergency departments, 2008–2010; Table 1 calls them amphetamine-related presentations (255 of 1,347). Whether the broader scope lies in the exposure or in the denominator (1,347 may be drug-related presentations rather than all attendees) cannot be told from the review; either way the 18.9% is not comparable with the other rows.

risk_of_bias.note: Overall critically low agreed: critical items 2, 4, 7, 11 and 15 are not met, which settles the rating whatever is decided on items 13 and 14. Instrument AMSTAR 2 matches the design. Domain differences below do not change the overall.

risk_of_bias_domains.note: Close call, as the card says (outcomes undefined, comparator only for demographics).
Strict but correct: AMSTAR 2 partial yes requires the language restriction to be justified.

AMSTAR 2 partial yes requires populations, interventions, comparators, outcomes and research designs all to be described; the card's own note says Table 1 does not give the designs (only Pasic is labelled case-control), and comparators are not described.

A further reason: Richards et al. (1999a) enters the prevalence, sex and age pools with all 32,617 visits, so about 29,500 unscreened attendees count as methamphetamine-negative in the sex and age comparisons (Figures 3–4).

risk_of_bias_domains.domain: 12. Impact of risk of bias on pooled results

risk_of_bias_domains.note: Close call. AMSTAR 2 gives yes when the review discusses the likely impact of risk of bias on its results; the critical-reflection paragraph (p. 10) does this (self-report, 72-hour screens, poly-drug use, under-reporting, intoxication against withdrawal). That the abstract does not carry it through is an interpretation gap rather than this item.

Close call. Sources were investigated (measurement method, setting), but the impact was not discussed: the Discussion presents an 11% average (p. 8) without saying what a four-fold difference by measurement method, and no heterogeneity statistic for the main pool, mean for that figure.

interpretation_gap.note: Substantial agreed; the 'catalyst' quotation is verbatim (p. 10) and the 'nearly half acutely psychotic' figure matches no study (Pasic 80%, others 12%). One addition: the Discussion's statement that people presenting with methamphetamine use were 10 years younger, citing Figure 4 (p. 8), rests on mean ages (28.4 against 38.4) whose source, SDs and method are not given; Figure 4 shows only odds ratios.

missed: Denominators that were not tested (Figure 2, p. 7; Table 1, p. 6): the Results say 120,111 attendees 'were tested' (p. 7), but nine of the 17 pooled studies used self-report, and Richards et al. (1999a) enters Figure 2 with all 32,617 emergency visits (461, 1.4%) although Table 1 gives 461 of 3,102 urine screens (14.9%) for the same year. The same all-visits figure is used in the sex pool (295 of 17,016 men, 166 of 15,601 women; Figure 3) and the age pool (461 against 32,156 'methamphetamine-negative'; Figure 4), so unscreened attendees count as negative. This lowers the pooled 11.3%, may lower the toxicology subgroup if Richards 1999a was counted there, and biases the sex and age comparisons for the largest single study.
Card field comparison.matching: 'Pasic et al. (2007) used matched samples ... which makes its sex and age contributions products of the design' is not supported; see reporting issue 10.

Mean ages 28.4 against 38.4 years (abstract; p. 8): no source, SD, number of studies or pooling method is given, and Figure 4 contains only odds ratios; the card reports the means without this caveat (sample.demographics, key finding 10).
